To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

deep neural networks can explain a significant amount of activity in the mouse brain, that convolution is necessary for explaining activity in mouse visual cortex, and that self-supervised and normalization-free models perform better than their supervised counterparts.
1) Deep convolutional networks are better at explaining the visual system than previous work suggested.

1) deep neural networks are capable of modeling rodent visual cortex; 2) the most predictive models of rodent visual cortex have convolutional architectures; 3) the most predictive convolutional models are those trained to predict visual stimuli; and 4) the most predictive model of rodent visual activity is a vision transformer trained to predict visual inputs.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions: How well do deep networks fare as models for the visual cortex? Can they be used to explain neural activity in the visual cortex? If so, which networks and which tasks? How do we measure their performance? What do we learn from their successes and failures?

the following overarching questions: How well do deep networks fare as models for the rodent visual system? What are the properties of the best models? What are the best models? How do the best models compare to models of the human visual system?
how well modern deep neural networks can be used to model the visual system of a mammalian model organism with a perceptual ecology and physiology markedly different from that of primates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
deep neural networks can be used as models of mouse vision, and that they are capable of modeling the visual system to a degree that is at least as good as that of previous attempts, if not better.
the best performing models of mouse vision, as measured by the Allen Brain Observatory, are convolutional neural networks trained on natural images.
deep neural network models can explain the activity of individual neurons, but not necessarily the population activity, in mouse visual cortex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can now use modern neural networks to explain the activity of the mouse visual cortex with more precision than we can explain the activity of primate visual areas.
the best models of primate visual system are also the best models of rodent visual cortex.
deep neural networks can indeed model the mouse visual system, though they do not yet match the level of performance we have come to expect in primate visual cortex.
The main takeaway from our work is that
deep networks can indeed be used to explain the activity of neurons in rodent visual cortex, but that the choice of model architecture is critical for this to happen.
, with the right models, deep neural networks can be powerful tools in the modeling of mouse visual cortical function.
the Allen Brain Observatory dataset is a rich and powerful tool that can be used to benchmark and compare the performance of different models of the brain.
